title: Ibn Sina
hookLine: the Canon of Medicine, a textbook in Europe and Asia for centuries

lines: A CHEAP VOLUME IN THE MARKET.
cards: A young man is stuck. He has read a book of Greek philosophy over and over, until he knows the words by heart, and still it makes no sense. He gives up.
Then one afternoon, in the booksellers' market of Bukhara, a seller pushes a cheap little volume into his hands. He doesn't want it. The seller insists: the owner needs the money.
He buys it, takes it home, and it turns out to be a short explanation of the very book that had defeated him. Suddenly, it opens.
He says, in his own account, that he was so glad he went out and gave alms to the poor in thanks. The young man was Ibn Sina.

teach.h: A LIFE TOLD TO A STUDENT.
teach.b: That story comes from Ibn Sina's own short account of his life, told to a student. He describes a boyhood of learning the Qur'an, then law, logic and mathematics, then medicine, which he says he didn't find hard.

teach.h: STUCK? GO TO THE MOSQUE AND PRAY.
teach.b: And something else: when a problem defeated him, he would go to the mosque and pray, asking God to open what was closed, then go back to work, sometimes into the night. Faith and study, in his telling, were one effort.
His great medical book is al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, the Canon of Medicine.
Qanun means a rule, a standard.

The Canon tried to gather what was known about the body into one ordered whole: how health is kept, how illness shows itself, which medicines do what, and how to treat each part of the body, head to foot, so medicine could be studied in order.
Historians describe the Canon being taught as a textbook for a long time, in Muslim lands and, in Latin translation, in the universities of Europe: read by students who would never meet.
And its opening defines medicine as the knowledge of the body in health and in illness, so that health can be kept, and restored when it's lost. Keeping comes before restoring.
Whole sections deal with sleep, food, exercise, air, the state of your mind. The body is cared for every day, not only rescued when it breaks.

how: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was studied as a medical textbook, and in his own account of his life he describes turning to prayer in the mosque when a problem would not open.

games.q: you're young Ibn Sina. you've read a hard book again and again and it still makes no sense. a bookseller offers you a cheap volume you don't want. what do you do?
o: walk on; you've given up on the subject.
buy it to help the owner who needs the money.
argue the price down to nothing.
games.why: he bought it, and it explained the very book that had defeated him. he gave alms in thanks.

practice: Sit tall, feet on the floor, and move your attention slowly from your head down to your feet, the way the Canon moves through the body: head and eyes, neck and shoulders, chest, stomach, legs, feet.
Where is something asking for care: water, a walk, an earlier night, a real meal? If you pray, you can thank God for the body you were given; if not, just thank it yourself.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Sina. A physician and philosopher who prayed when he was stuck and wrote the Canon of Medicine, one ordered book of the body. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the canon. One ordered book, for keeping health and restoring it. Until tomorrow.
